Three of the directors come from Tesla: Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, and Jack Hartung. Two come from SpaceX: Roelof Botha and Randy Glein. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter regarding this development. Reuters could not immediately verify the report at the time it was published, and neither SpaceX nor Tesla responded to requests for comment.
items.title: SpaceX and Tesla Appoint Five Directors for Merger Negotiations

items.summary: According to a report in The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the discussion, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang disclosed additional extramarital affairs beyond the three previously reported during a marathon meeting with the company's board on Sunday. At 63 years old, he reportedly expressed regret over his conduct during several hours of discussions with directors. The board spoke to him about the importance of transparency and candor before concluding that reinstating him as chief executive was the best course of action.
items.title: Jensen Huang Disclosed Additional Affairs Before Nvidia Reinstates Him as CEO

items.summary: Joshua S. Gans and Richard T. Holden, in their NBER Working Paper 36048 (2026), present a criterion for when the decisions of an AI's principal are sufficient on their own to align the agent without additional evidence-gathering. Their framework addresses how AI agents learn what principals want from observing which choices those principals make. The authors argue that cautious actions—such as deferring to a person—typically partition a principal's possible actions into distinct blocks, and decisions alone suffice exactly when the same costless evidence is optimal in every such block. When this condition fails, an agent can nonetheless act as its principal would while collecting misleading or incorrect evidence; notably, greater capability may convert that evidentiary error into wrong actions. The authors illustrate their point by noting that choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions fail to capture.
items.title: Gans and Holden Propose a Criterion for When Revealed Preferences Suffice in AI Alignment

items.summary: A study by Jingjing Chen, Jianlei Han, Shing-Yi Wang, and Yongxiang Wang examines a 1492 Ming dynasty reform that shifted military grain delivery from salt merchants to a state relay system featuring prefecture-to-prefecture handovers along fixed routes. The authors argue that bureaucratic rules intended to improve accountability can undermine state effectiveness. According to the study, court records after the reform documented more supply shortages at formerly merchant-supplied garrisons than at state-supplied ones. Analyzing 406 defensive battles against foreign invaders, the researchers found that the reform reduced victory rates near these garrisons. The declines were largest where resupply mattered most—longer wars and walled-city defenses—and where the state's rules were most costly, specifically routes crossing more prefectures or exposed to floods, droughts, or rugged terrain.
items.title: Ming Dynasty Military Logistics Reform Reduced Battle Victory Rates

items.summary: Channel 4 has suffered a significant blow after Unilever cut almost all of its television advertising spending in favour of online influencer marketing. Guardian analysis based on industry sources shows Unilever's UK TV media spend has plummeted by just over 50% so far this year compared with the same period in 2025, though figures indicate it spent about £92m on UK TV advertising last year and as much as £122m in 2023. Channel 4 was proportionally the hardest hit, with Unilever slashing approximately 92% of its spending with the broadcaster, which is making record job cuts amid a tough advertising market. Sky took a 44% hit while ITV experienced a 42% fall; although these were smaller proportional declines than Channel 4's, they represented bigger absolute losses because Unilever spends more money with them in spend terms.
items.title: Unilever Cuts UK TV Ad Spend, Devastating Channel 4

items.summary: A vendor at the 13,000-foot-high Rohatang Pass in Himachal Pradesh reportedly generates daily sales of ₹14,000 to ₹15,000 from selling Maggi noodles and tea. According to the shopkeeper cited by content creator Harsh Chauhan—who shared a viral video discussing the business—the store sells about 60-70 plates of Maggi (priced at ₹100 each) and roughly 200 cups of tea (₹40 each) daily, yielding approximately ₹6,000 to ₹7,000 from Maggi and around ₹8,000 from tea. If this sales rate continued consistently, the monthly turnover could reach about ₹4.65 lakh; however, after deducting expenses for goods, transport, staff, and other costs, actual profit would be lower than gross sales.
items.title: Rohatang Pass Vendor's Daily Sales Surpass Monthly Figures in Himaachal Pradesh

items.summary:
Los Angeles' long-awaited LAX people mover project, officially named SkyLink, has gone off track despite its elevated tracks and train cars being operational. The less than 2.5 miles (4km) rail line broke ground in 2019 under then-mayor Eric Garcetti as part of a $30bn plan to modernize LAX, aiming to provide direct terminal-to-terminal connections with congestion relief for the airport's millions of annual visitors.

The project has exceeded its budget by more than $1bn and is expected to overshoot its intended 2023 opening date by four years. City officials report it is 99% complete, but final testing requiring at least 30 consecutive days of uninterrupted operation has stretched beyond 200 days. An estimated opening was pushed back multiple times to March 2027 after Linxs moved the projected date again last week.

The project began as a public-private partnership between Los Angeles World Airports (Lawa) and contractor LAX Integrated Express Solutions (Linxs), which signed a contract in 2019 to design, construct, operate and maintain SkyLink for 30 years. The initial price tag was $1.9bn; disputes over design codes led Linxs to submit hundreds of change orders, culminating in a settlement granting an additional $550m as costs ballooned to nearly $3bn.

A Los Angeles county civil grand jury released its report last year concluding that Linxs took the airport authority for about $880m because city officials wrote up the contract poorly. The contractor allegedly leveraged contractual intricacies by barraging departments with change orders and delaying work, while also using political pressure around major sporting events as leverage.

In July, Linxs sued the city over alleged breaches of contract including faulty electrical equipment that delayed key testing more than 140 days, though airport officials called these false legal assertions. Under settlement terms, Linxs must deliver a passenger-ready system by December 8; if it misses this date, which appears likely to happen, the project could face further disarray.

Eli Lipmen of Move LA described the project as an embarrassment and warned of potentially having a $3bn distressed asset on their hands. Nithya Raman, who defeated incumbent mayor Karen Bass in the mayoral race, held up SkyLink as a symbol of city hall dysfunction and called for investigation into alleged criminal wrongdoing.

The 11-acre LAX/Metro Transit Center opened June 2025 but remains separate from the people mover. UCLA's Juan Matute intends to study how this public-private partnership derailed, noting that outside oversight could help prevent similar mistakes in future projects.
items.title: LAX's SkyLink People Mover Derailed by Delays, Cost Overruns

items.summary: Hours before Nvidia reinstated ousted CEO Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump called into the company's Sunday board meeting to argue for his return. The direct engagement by Trump — first reported by Semafor and confirmed by multiple sources — underscores how he has redefined the role of the US government in private enterprise. Vice President JD Vance and other administration members also became involved in Nvidia's inner workings, even as some members of Trump's own party questioned whether reinstating Huang poses a national security risk.
items.title: Trump Pressured Nvidia Board to Reinstated Jensen Huang

items.summary: High street retailer Next announced that some of its data has been accessed in a cyber breach affecting a third-party online supplier. The company, headquartered in Enderby, Leicestershire, said it was informed by the supplier about an incident involving "unauthorised access to certain benign data relating to Next." Next stated there was no evidence that customers' personal data had been compromised and described the affected information as limited in nature, concluding that based on its current assessment it cannot be used to facilitate fraud against customers or the company. The firm said it took immediate steps to investigate the incident with the supplier while investigations continued, treating the situation "with the utmost seriousness" and working with the supplier, police, and regulators.
items.title: Next Reports Cyber Breach at Third-Party Supplier

items.summary: Eleven days after resigning over revelations of extramarital affairs — including one with a former executive of Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer under US investigation — Jensen Huang was unanimously voted back by Nvidia's board on Monday to serve again as chief executive, president and board director. The board cited input from senior US government officials that his return posed no national security risk, prompting shares to jump nearly 32% in a session adding close to $1 trillion in market value, the company's best day since May 2003.
items.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, sparking rally in Europe's AI stocks

items.summary: Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that China will actively support Nepal's post-disaster reconstruction efforts, helping affected residents rebuild their homes and return to normal life as early as possible. Speaking in response to a question about Nepal's planned fund-raising summit following the devastating late-August floods, Guo noted that China immediately announced emergency assistance and rescue cooperation after the mudslide disaster in northern Nepal. He described China and Nepal as friendly neighbors connected by mountains and rivers, and said Beijing provided cash aid, five batches of emergency relief supplies, sent over 20 experts specializing in tunnel rescue and forensic identification, and ongoing meteorological, hydrological and geological data. Guo added that people from various sectors in China also extended a helping hand to the affected population. He noted that the disaster has caused severe damage and reconstruction faces enormous challenges, with China closely following developments and offering its sympathy for Nepal over the disaster. Guo said China will also help Nepal improve its disaster prevention and mitigation capabilities to better address risks brought by natural disasters.
items.title: China Promises Support for Nepal's Post-Flood Reconstruction

items.summary: Malaysia announced it will send thousands of migrants and refugees back to Myanmar, even while acknowledging that many asylum seekers in the country had been victims of atrocities carried out by the junta in Naypyidaw. The announcement came just days after the UN's International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.
items.title: Malaysia to Deport Thousands of Migrants Back to Myanmar as PM Acknowledges Junta Atrocities

items.summary: Saurav Das, a leader of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from boarding a flight to the UK on Tuesday morning after his passport was flagged. He had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about Gen Z-led protests and also planned to address events at universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh, writing that he believed an 'anti-intellectual government' feared his presence at these institutions. The BBC has contacted the federal home ministry, Delhi police, and airport officials for comment; a home ministry spokesperson directed those inquiries toward the relevant authorities rather than addressing Das's allegations directly. Ratna Singh, another CJP leader, said she was also invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected days earlier, adding that how Das was denied boarding raises 'deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country.' Das rose to prominence after Gen Z-led protests earlier this year. The CJP began as satire before becoming a youth-led pressure group; in July, CJP-prospearheaded protests over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, and in October CJP leaders including Das were among thousands detained for attempting to hold protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged electoral roll irregularities that Kumar and the Election Commission have denied. That same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka were jailed for seven days after trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke wrote on X that if Das 'had looted a bank or committed financial fraud,' he might still have been allowed to fly to London, referencing billionaire bank-loan defaulters who left India. The report notes other recent instances of people being prevented from boarding flights: Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from Arunachal Pradesh, was stopped in September 2025 before a flight to Dublin, and investigative journalist Rana Ayyub was barred at Mumbai airport in March 2022 before speaking at events on media freedom.}
items.title: India's 'Cockroach' Party Leader Says Passport Flagged, Blocking UK Travel

items.summary: At the Tainan International Travel Fair, which ran from Friday to Monday in southern Taiwan's city of Tainan, cultural tours to mainland China drew visitor interest. The Kaohsiung office of the mainland-based Association for Tourism Exchange Across the Taiwan Straits showcased cultural relics and scenic spots from five mainland provinces at its booth. A female visitor surnamed Hu picked up several brochures and considered a trip to Shandong Province, which she associated with Qufu, the birthplace of Confucius, and Weifang, known as the kite capital; she said she planned to add more stops based on the materials. Another visitor surnamed Chu, who came from nearby Chiayi, had originally intended to see giant pandas but was advised by booth staff to also visit Chengdu's Wuhou Shrine, honoring Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang of the Three Kingdoms period (220-280), a site she now planned to visit after having read 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms' as a child. The article notes that despite a ban on group tours to the mainland and a travel alert issued by Democratic Progressive Party authorities, travel from Taiwan continues to grow: island tourism figures show residents made 2.49 million trips to the mainland in January through August this year, up 19.63% from the same period last year. Wang Hsien-wen, vice director of the Tainan Association of Travel Agents, attributed rising interest partly to social media communities discussing mainland tours that attract thousands of users sharing experiences and tips. The article also reports that travel has become easier as permit applications are facilitated for Taiwan residents: first-time visitors pay no application fee, 100 ports can issue single-entry permits on arrival, and various attractions offer discounted or free admission; a visitor surnamed Lin from Kaohsiung said he was surprised by how easy it would be to travel there. Lin added that as a fan of mainland historical dramas, which he had watched several times, he planned to visit Beijing, Nanjing, and other historic cities to experience traditional Chinese culture firsthand.
items.title: Cultural Tours to Mainland China Draw Interest at Tainan Travel Fair

items.summary: Russian negotiators, having agreed to new peace talks with Ukrainian and American representatives earlier this month, suddenly requested that the discussions also address the broader European security order. The text characterizes this move as an attempt by Russia to divert attention from what it describes as the urgent need for a ceasefire in President Vladimir Putin's war against Ukraine after almost five years of conflict. While U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff reportedly appeared willing to accommodate the Russian proposal, European observers rejected it, pointing out that an agreed European security order already exists—one to which Russia is a signatory—and arguing that discussions should instead focus on Russia's alleged blatant violations of that existing framework.
items.title: Russia Diverts Peace Talks Toward European Security Order

items.summary: A new study published in Canid Biology & Conservation quantifies how rare bush dogs (Speothos venaticus) are in the wild. Robert Wallace and colleagues at the Wildlife Conservation Society analyzed 25 years of camera-trap data from 97 sites across seven South American countries, examining more than 2.1 million photographs taken over 611,159 camera-trap nights. Bush dogs appeared on just 12 occasions in this dataset.
items.title: New Study Quantifies Extreme Rarity of Bush Dogs in the Wild

items.summary: The Tripoli-based Libyan foreign ministry condemned a Ukrainian drone attack on two Russian ships near the eastern city of Benghazi over the weekend, demanding an explanation from Ukraine. Separately, South Korean authorities said Tuesday that several Russian military aircraft had breached its air defence zone, correcting an earlier alert that had reported a North Korean plane incursion. Finland summoned Russia's ambassador after a suspected violation of Finnish airspace by a Russian helicopter and following a Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland over recent days. Additionally, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said intelligence indicated Russia planned new strikes on Ukraine and urged the United States and other countries to take note as air defence system supplies depend on their decisions.
items.title: Tripoli Demands Explanation from Kyiv After Drone Strike on Russian Ships in Libyan Waters

items.summary: Japan's logistics industry has long relied on independent delivery networks, with freight vehicles operating in the same areas from multiple companies. Loading efficiency of these vehicles has remained around 40% of their carrying capacity for roughly the past 15 years due to smaller shipments and underused return trips, a condition that is both inefficient and hinders efforts to reduce carbon dioxide emissions. A chronic shortage of truck drivers—driven by Japan's declining and aging population—and new regulations introduced in 2024 aimed at improving working hours and conditions for drivers have further worsened the situation, making insufficient transportation capacity a critical challenge nationwide.
items.title: Seino Holdings Partners With Competitors to Improve Logistics Efficiency and Reduce Emissions

items.summary:
As the annual pygmy blue whale migration intensifies in Timor-Leste's waters, conservationists warn that a booming swim-with-whales industry is increasingly disrupting migrating whales despite new government guidelines. The number of operators has grown markedly this season, with fewer whales passing through the Ombai-Wetar Strait likely due to cooler El Niño and positive Indian Ocean Dipole conditions delaying migration (Professor Karen Edyvane). This surge has intensified competition among operators charging tourists $250-350 a day for encounters with only a few hundred pygmy blue whales that pass through annually.

The new guidelines, released Sept. 30 by the Timorese government and Conservation International with Australian assistance and technical input from whale experts including Edyvane, establish rules on approaching distances, speed limits, and prohibit chasing or blocking animals' paths (Delio da Costa). However, repeated breaches have exposed a lack of enforcement in an industry without a formal regulatory framework — no operator has been apprehended for misconduct since the industry emerged about a decade ago. Documented violations include boats cutting across whales' paths, operators pursuing mothers with calves, too many swimmers in the water at once (Tom Quinney), and one tourist swimming with a whale on a jet ski.

Marine biologist Ywen Mieybégué identified drone footage of Timor Sunshine Divers speeding into the path of a female pygmy blue whale and her calf. Separated calves face greater vulnerability to predation, injury, and impaired growth (Quinney). Edyvane has documented underweight whales with visible ribs and vertebrae, suspecting ocean warming disrupts upwellings sustaining their food supply.

Disagreements persist between operators and scientists over approach practices. Simon Jeffrey, co-owner of Dive Timor Lorosae, argues positioning a boat ahead of a whale is acceptable if the vessel stays still and swimmers remain motionless (Jeffrey), but Capri Jolliffe insists on respecting the 30 m / 100 ft minimum distance between swimmers and whales as globally-accepted standard for responsible whale watching. Jeffrey also disagrees with mandatory distances, considering closer encounters acceptable when a whale approaches rather than vice versa.

Conservationists and operators increasingly call for licensing, monitoring, boat number caps, surveillance, mandatory training paid by permit fees (Edyvane), and greater Timorese participation in an industry dominated by foreign firms. Mieybégué wants regulations introduced as soon as possible starting with a cap on boats allowed on the water. The government says it has yet to receive any whale-related complaints through its general tourism channels, though photographer Ollie Clarke wrote an open letter last December after witnessing multiple operators flouting rules.

Timor-Leste's director general for fisheries, Akasio dos Santos, said a draft law addressing unlicensed operators could be submitted for review as soon as next year. Under the draft, only licensed operators meeting technical and legal requirements who paid license fees would operate, and only tourists paying sustainable tourism fees could swim with whales (dos Santos). The government still needs to determine which ministry — Tourism and Environment or Agriculture/Livestock/Fisheries/Forestry — leads regulations.

The article references Tonga's $12 million whale-tourism industry as an example where complaints led to a tour operator suspension in October. Edyvane noted Timor could develop the world's most responsible whale-watching industry but must prioritize including more Timorese in management and permit processes.
items.title: Timor-Leste Issues Whale-Watching Guidelines Amid Booming, Unregulated Industry

items.summary: After 44 hours of overtime on top of two weeks of negotiations, COP31 concluded in Antalya without producing a climate agreement. The proposed pact—drafted by co-hosts Türkiye and Australia—promoted carbon capture technology while omitting any commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, the leading cause of climate change. This meant it did not reference TAFF (transitioning away from fossil fuels), which had been agreed at COP28 in Dubai.
items.title: COP31 Ends Without a Climate Agreement After Fossil Fuel Dispute

items.summary:
The latest Rental Affordability Index, produced by CGS Economics and Planning and National Shelter, found Canberra has the most "acceptable" rental market among Australia's capital cities, with the average renting household spending 22.6 per cent of its income on rent — a marked improvement from being ranked as one of the two least affordable cities in 2022. Perth currently holds the title of least affordable city, followed by Hobart and Sydney.

The study measured affordability relative to household incomes and found Canberra has the highest average rental household gross income at $142,658 per year. SGS Economics principal Ellen Witte attributed this partly to rent stabilisation measures introduced by the ACT government in 2019: annual rent increases capped at 10 per cent above CPI growth with eight weeks' notice required. "There are some guardrails now ... and so it's still possible as a landlord to increase your rents, but not in an excessive way," Witte said.

Witte noted that five of the seven capital cities were tracking poorly while only Canberra (improving) and Melbourne (stabilising) were getting better — "it just happens to be so that those are the two jurisdictions that put in place some regulations around rent increases." However, ACT Shelter chief executive Corinne Dobson warned the positive headline figures "only tell half of the story," describing a "two-tier" rental system where high average incomes mask severe stress for low-income earners and students.

The study found hospitality workers renting in Canberra spent an average of 38 per cent of their income on rent, while early childhood educators spent 37 per cent. A person on JobSeeker payments with rental assistance sees 99 per cent of their income go to rent, and median rents took up 62 per cent of a single pensioner's aged pension income.

Dobson said low-income renters face the highest rates of rental stress in Canberra — "the case for well over a decade" — while student Dylan Adams has struggled to find quality housing amid mould, insufficient bathrooms, and poor kitchens. Witte described tenants as being "between a rock and a hard place," citing parents skipping meals so children can eat, people skipping medicine or turning homeless, and even employed individuals living out of their cars."
items.title: Canberra Tops Rental Affordability Index Despite 'Two-Tier' System for Low-Income Renters

visual.alt: Bar chart. Average renting household 22.6 %; Hospitality workers (average) 38 %; Early childhood educators 37 %; JobSeeker recipient with rental assistance 99 %; Single pensioner's aged pension (median rent) 62 %.

items.summary: Former claims investigator Ashley Austin alleges that multi-billion-dollar insurer Suncorp fostered a 'toxic' corporate culture incentivizing staff to deny or minimize home insurance claims. Speaking to ABC's 7.30, Ms Austin said she was rewarded for increasing company profits by reducing claim values at customers' expense, describing the practice as driven by monetary targets rather than customer assistance: 'It's all about profit, making money, business.' She recounted that staff were given $50 gift cards for declining the most claims by Friday 3pm and described joking in work group chats about scripted responses to distressed claimants. Ms Austin said customers sometimes threatened suicide over the stress of their experiences, with investigators requesting additional documentation such as psychiatric clearances to delay processing.
items.title: Whistleblower accuses Suncorp of encouraging home insurance claim denials

items.summary: On November 19, leaders of China, Russia, and the United States met for the first trilateral summit in Shenzhen, where they adopted the China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace. In its opening lines, the Russian and US presidents expressed appreciation to China for hosting what they called a 'historic trilateral Summit.' The declaration contains four points: as permanent members of the Security Council, the three countries committed to reforming the United Nations; they plan to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products 'for the benefit of all nations'; they affirmed state consent and immunity of state officials while stating that the International Criminal Court and similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction; and they reaffirmed that 'a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,' agreeing to a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation. The author, Solomzi Tshona—an Industrial Engineering Researcher at EITIE research group at Constructor University in Bremen and PhD candidate in Development Economics at the Global School of Leadership, Renmin University of China—frames this summit as reflecting two competing visions of global power: one treating every gain as someone else's loss, and another holding that a country's progress is secure only when its neighbors progress together. Tshona attributes these views to himself rather than to CGTN.
items.title: China Hosts First China-Russia-US Trilateral Summit in Shenzhen

items.summary: Demonstrators rallied in Brussels carrying placards warning that 'Rent is eating into our wages' and 'The rich earn more, the workers pay more,' to oppose around €10 billion in proposed spending cuts before clashes broke out with riot police. Officers responded with tear gas, water cannons, and charges as a car burned and arrests were made amid plumes of smoke. For protesters already squeezed by high energy costs, inflation, and shrinking purchasing power, the planned savings threaten to place an unfair burden on the lowest-paid while undermining social security, employment support, and help for families. The street anger occurred on the very day Prime Minister Bart De Wever met King Philippe to update him on strained talks over Belgium's 2027 budget. Having set a year-end deadline for coalition partners to sign off on the cuts and warned that the government could collapse if negotiations fail, De Wever now faces sharpening resistance both inside parliament and on the streets as he seeks to reconcile fiscal discipline with demands to protect living standards.
items.title: Belgian Workers March Against Spending Cuts Amid Rising Living Costs

items.summary: Tensions are escalating in Libya after an attack on two vessels off the coast of Benghazi, one of which was a Russian warship. Naval forces in eastern Libya have been placed on maximum alert following the incident. Kyiv claims to have carried out an operation targeting Russian military assets, while the United Nations is calling for an independent investigation and warning that the Russia-Ukraine conflict could expand onto Libyan soil. Separately, China has increased its diplomatic engagement in the Horn of Africa amid growing tensions in the Red Sea and Middle East; Chinese envoys traveled to Ethiopia, Djibouti, Egypt, and Eritrea to promote dialogue, regional security, and cooperation among countries in the region. On the climate front, COP31 concluded in Turkey without a major agreement after negotiations stalled over fossil fuels, climate finance, and carbon capture, renewing calls for reform of a process widely seen as paralysed by its consensus rule. In Central Africa, efforts are underway to ease tensions between Nairobi and Kinshasa; Kenyan President William Ruto and DR Congo's President Félix Tshisekedi met in Oyo, Republic of the Congo, under the mediation of Denis Sassou-Nguesso, with both leaders pledging to prioritise dialogue and strengthen economic and healthcare cooperation. In Cairo, an annual honey festival is celebrating Egyptian producers while raising awareness about different varieties; the sector is expanding, with more than 20,000 tonnes produced this year and several thousand tonnes exported.
items.title: Russia Claims Attack on Libyan Vessels Including Warship; COP31 Ends Without Major Agreement

items.summary: On Monday (23 November 2026), UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that artificial intelligence is advancing at extraordinary speed and amplifying cybersecurity risks, manipulation, and misuse, while urging countries to act now so every nation can manage the technology safely. Speaking at a news conference during the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety in Barbados, Guterres said recent technological outages and cyberattacks have exposed vulnerabilities in digital systems that societies increasingly depend on, noting that protections remain fragmented and too often reactive. He emphasized that many countries still lack the tools, knowledge, and capacity to assess AI systems entering their markets or protect people when problems arise, calling this gap a priority that must be closed so every country can manage AI safely with credible, independent ways to evaluate powerful AI systems. Guterres urged states, the private sector, financial institutions, foundations, and other donors to increase investments in AI capacity-building and contribute urgently to funding for developing minimum AI capacity in Global South regions, stressing that because risks are global, responses must be global. Barbados Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley echoed the call, warning that if AI capacity remains concentrated in a few regions existing inequalities would widen further; she pointed to needed investments in infrastructure, data sets, skills, and models respecting local values, saying AI innovation must advance human rights, support sustainable development, enable people's agency over their future, reflect global diversity, build locally for sovereignty, and avoid the commoditization of human beings as data packs serving only a few.
items.title: UN Chief Warns AI Risks Growing as He Urges Global Action to Close Capacity Gap

items.summary: In the 2026 midterm elections, Democrats won the U.S. House by their largest margin in half a century and secured the biggest majority since the early 1990s. Fifty-six percent of voters chose Democratic candidates compared with 42% for Republicans, producing a 14-point gap that NPR identified as the widest such advantage in 50 years.
items.title: Democrats Win Largest House Majority in 50 Years as COP31 Ends Without a Deal

items.summary:
Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician and Nepal's first-time prime minister, made his inaugural state visit to India this week, marking a departure from the country's history of revolving coalition governments. As a young leader with a strong electoral mandate, Shah represents a new political force in Kathmandu whose bilateral trip carried significant weight given long-standing economic strain, August's devastating flash floods, and public hopes for jobs, investment, and better governance.

Shah prioritized securing Indian support to safeguard Nepal's flood recovery. The August disaster claimed more than 1,450 lives, with 5,745 people missing or unaccounted for. The floods swept away roads, bridges, hydropower projects, and settlements, leaving reconstruction bills estimated at around $4.8 billion (about €4.4 billion). At a joint press briefing after talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday, Modi announced a $1.63 billion package to help rebuild flood-hit areas and upgrade infrastructure — roughly $380 million as a grant, with the remainder as a concessional loan.

The two countries agreed to deepen cooperation across trade, investment, connectivity, people-to-people ties, educational and innovation partnerships, energy and infrastructure collaboration, market access, and additional air and port access for landlocked Nepal. They also launched a new long-term vision aimed at strengthening economic integration and development.

Despite the focus on economics, unresolved territorial disputes persist over Kalapani, Lipulekh, and Limpiyadhura in northwestern Nepal. As mayor of Kathmandu, Shah raised these border issues to boost his nationalist image; however, his India visit steered clear of such contentious matters. Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Foreign Minister of Nepal, told DW that while the visit could be a good starting point for resolving border issues, "the new government didn't show interest or the guts to address this." Ashok Swain, head of the Department of Peace and Conflict Research at Sweden's Uppsala University, added that Nepal's territorial disputes, concerns over the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, and its economic and transit dependence on India need addressing. He argued Shah's biggest opportunity is to transform Nepal's location between India and China from a strategic vulnerability into an economic and diplomatic asset.

Constantino Xavier, a senior fellow at the Center for Social and Economic Progress in New Delhi, cautioned against expecting too much from a single visit, telling DW that "we need a big, long-term ambition coupled with small, short-term steps" while keeping economic cooperation central to relations. Whether the visit marks a tangible reset on the economic front will ultimately depend not on the number of agreements announced but on how they are implemented and whether both governments address the disputes that have long strained ties.
items.title: Nepal's New PM Balendra Shah Eyes Closer Ties with India Amid Lingering Disputes

items.summary: A judiciary official said Monday that Iranian courts have ordered the United States to pay $290 billion in damages for decades of actions against Iran. Hassan Abdolianpour, head of the judiciary's centre for lawyers, told state television: "We have secured court rulings in domestic courts awarding $290 billion in damages against the Americans." According to state TV, the ruling covers US actions going back decades.
items.title: Iranian Courts Order US to Pay $290 Billion in Damages

items.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX and Tesla have appointed five independent directors—three from Tesla (Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, and Jack Hartung) and two from SpaceX (Roelof Botha and Randy Glein)—to guide special committees handling merger negotiations, according to a report by The Financial Times on Tuesday. These appointments follow Musk's remarks during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call last month in which he described a merger uniting his AI, robotics, electric vehicle, and aerospace ambitions under one corporate structure as 'a good idea,' and confirmed that the companies had formed committees of independent directors to discuss the union. The FT report cited people familiar with the matter; Reuters could not immediately verify it, and neither company responded to requests for comment outside regular business hours. According to the report, the special committees have retained advisers—Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs for SpaceX, and Evercore for Tesla—to refine financial models that will underpin their negotiating positions in an all-stock merger, including analysis of which parts of the proposed conglomerate overlap. The potential combination faces steep regulatory hurdles over SpaceX's U.S. defense contracts and Tesla's reliance on China. Bloomberg had reported earlier this month that a deal could be announced as early as December, citing progress in negotiations.
items.title: SpaceX and Tesla Form Special Committees for Merger Talks

items.summary:
Nvidia's board reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO at the urging of President Donald Trump, less than two weeks after he resigned following revelations that he had extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of ties to Beijing. The alleged relationships triggered resignations and investigations by the US securities regulator (SEC) and FBI, congressional hearings, an internal review by Nvidia's independent directors, and proposed investor lawsuits.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful but has not publicly detailed the individual relationships; China denied espionage allegations, and attempts to reach Alice Huang were unsuccessful. Nvidia stated that based on US government input it was confident "Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," a claim Trump backed in an interview with CNBC, saying Huang did nothing wrong.

Legal exposure remains significant despite the rehiring sparking a massive stock rally. An investor filed a derivative lawsuit in federal court on November 11 seeking to hold the board liable for failing to oversee the business and Huang; attorney Lee Squitieri told Reuters that rehiring Huang does not change liability much, as problems extend beyond export control violations to include poor succession planning and weak governance. Nvidia has officers' and directors' insurance coverage of up to $950 million.

Trump's statement could strengthen the board's legal defenses by suggesting no prosecution for export control violations is likely during his administration, though the statute of limitations extends past January 2029 when he leaves office, and a new attorney general could reopen an investigation. Trump also could preemptively pardon Huang to avoid future prosecution.

State investigations continue: Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said Monday her probe into whether Huang's actions harmed state pension funds would proceed through a consumer protection lens; California Attorney General Rob Bonta served Nvidia an investigative subpoena on November 19 regarding whether China obtained advanced chips or confidential information. The SEC is investigating potential accounting issues, though Reuters could not determine whether Trump's intervention changed that federal probe.

A proposed class action filed in San Jose on November 9 alleges the company and Huang defrauded shareholders by concealing the relationship with Alice Huang and her former company Megaspeed; stock fell around 20 per cent from its peak to the end of the class period, a decline of about $1 trillion in market value. A rebound could undermine the lawsuit's value if shares continue rising, as US securities law caps shareholder damages when stocks recover within 90 days.
items.title: Nvidia and its board still face legal risks after Jensen Huang's return

items.summary: Nvidia executive Jensen Huang, 63, returned to lead the AI chipmaker after being greeted with cheers and chants of "Jensen!" at his welcome. In a video shared on social media by Ming-Yu Liu, Nvidia's vice president of research, Huang addressed employees, apologizing for mistakes he said he had made and thanking them for giving him another chance. He stated that he would work to become a better CEO the second time around. Nvidia's official X account marked his return with a post reading "He's back," along with an image of the welcome celebrations shared without a caption.
items.title: Jensen Huang Returns to Nvidia as CEO

items.summary: In an X post, Kotak described Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia leadership as 'one of the most consequential decisions in the history of world markets,' pointing to a $1 trillion recovery in Nvidia's market capitalization and a $4 trillion recovery in US market capitalization that he linked to America's ambition to stay ahead in the AI race. He characterized the situation with the analogy, 'When elephants dance, everyone moves to give space!' The reinstatement followed one of the most unusual leadership episodes in Nvidia's history: Huang stepped down on November 12, ending a 33-year tenure as CEO four days after acknowledging an affair with his wife, Lori. US intelligence agencies reportedly concluded Alice Huang was a Beijing intelligence asset who may have passed information to China; Nvidia maintained their interactions were routine business and that it had not shared classified information or compromised national security. The controversy also drew scrutiny of Megaspeed, whose reported assets rose to $3 billion in 2024 from $33 million in 2023 while revenue increased to $294 million from zero; the US Commerce Department began investigating whether it was diverting Nvidia's advanced processors to China, though no public finding has established a violation of export-control rules. Support for Huang emerged quickly: President Donald Trump said on November 17 he was open to his return after the chief 'learned a big lesson,' while Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney backed a 'Stand with Jensen' campaign supported by employees, investors, industry figures, and an online petition. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a leadership overhaul and argued Nvidia should look outside for its next chief executive; on November 18, chairman Harvey Jones said the board had unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him while continuing its search for a permanent successor. On November 23, however, Nvidia announced that its board had unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as president and CEO and a member of the board, citing his candour, leadership ability, input from senior US government officials, and confidence that his return posed no national security risk; Huang thanked the board, employees, shareholders, and industry partners. The investigations continue: Nvidia said its independent investigation into reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort would proceed, formed a separate National Security and Export Control Committee to oversee trade compliance, and is seeking to appoint a chief compliance officer. Meanwhile, Nvidia reported quarterly revenue of $116 billion—twice the level a year earlier—with data center revenue reaching $107.6 billion, and forecast $130 billion in revenue for the following quarter; Huang was also scheduled to face congressional questioning on December 1, with general counsel Tim Teter appearing the next day.
items.title: Kotak Frames Nvidia's $1 Trillion Market-Cap Recovery as a Landmark Moment Amid Jensen Huang's Reinstatement

items.summary: On Tuesday, November 24, Google denied reports of widespread layoffs in India following a post by X user Venkatesh Alla questioning the claims. The allegations stemmed from an anonymous post on the professional forum Blind describing alleged job cuts and termination notices across India-based cloud teams. In its response, posted directly to Alla's message by the official Google Cloud India account, the company stated that 'these rumors are totally inaccurate,' noting only that last week it made a small organizational change in India involving approximately 30 eliminated roles as part of work re-prioritization. The reply provided no details on affected teams or locations and did not address hiring plans or future cuts. Alla responded with skepticism, writing 'Pre-Prioritization?....Wow....' He also noted that the authors of two linked Blind threads had deleted them, while leaving it to others to judge whether Google's response was convincing. The anonymous poster described claims including sudden cuts across India Cloud teams with no performance link, 24-hour resign-or-get-fired ultimatums with one month severance, and rumors of January VEPs or layoffs in product and developer relations.
items.title: Google Denies 'Huge Layoffs' in India After Social Media Reports

items.summary: President Donald Trump claimed direct credit for reinstating Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive, telling CNBC that he spoke to the board and 'convinced them' during a Sunday meeting. His remarks followed a Semafor report indicating Trump dialed into the meeting to argue for Huang's return after directors requested assurance on national security concerns tied to an affair with a woman suspected by US officials of being a Chinese intelligence asset; Beijing denies the espionage allegation, and Nvidia said it had acted responsibly in removing Huang before reinstating him. On CNBC, Trump reframed the question as 'it's a threat to lose him,' added that Huang could travel freely to China, stated Huang 'did nothing wrong,' and predicted on Squawk on the Street that the scandal might prove a net positive because 'sex sells.' He subsequently posted an AI-altered Truth Social image placing Huang in a 2024 Butler, Pennsylvania post-shooting photograph with a bloodied face. Nvidia's stock rose 30% Monday, Semafor reported. Semafor also reported that Vice President JD Vance was involved and that the pitch cast Huang as a defender of open-source AI; Republican Sen. John Curtis questioned whether Huang poses no security risk, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren called the decision 'reckless,' Huang is due to face lawmakers behind closed doors on December 1, and the Justice Department continues investigating Megaspeed, Supermicro and Nvidia.
items.title: Trump Claims He Convinced Nvidia Board To Reinstate Jensen Huang As CEO

items.summary:
Kotak Mahindra Bank founder and director Uday Kotak described Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's chief executive officer as one of the most consequential decisions in global market history, posting on X that the move coincided with USD 1 trillion recovered in Nvidia's market capitalisation and USD 4 trillion across the US market. He attributed the decision to a political and economic agenda aimed at maintaining U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence while raising questions about rule flexibility amid great-power competition, writing: 'Jensen Huang coming back as NVIDIA CEO, is one of the most consequential decisions in the history of world markets' and adding that 'for global power play, the rules of the game are flexible.'

Nvidia's Board of Directors announced Monday it had unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as president and CEO with immediate effect after discussions and meetings with him. The board said it was satisfied with his candour and ability to lead the company and had received input from senior U.S. government levels before deciding. Huang's return followed his November 12 resignation amid allegations linked to an alleged Chinese espionage effort; interim CEO Colette Kress led the company during his departure while an independent board committee investigation continued.

The announcement triggered a sharp rally in Nvidia shares, which closed at USD 165.05 on Monday after gaining 31.48 per cent, and spurred Taiwan's benchmark Taiex to surge over 3,300 points in morning trade Tuesday—its biggest intraday gain on record as it crossed the 40,000-mark, according to Focus Taiwan.
items.title: Uday Kotak Calls Jensen Huang's Nvidia CEO Return a Defining Global Market Moment

items.summary: Senior Congress leader Sonia Gandhi has publicly reiterated her long-standing allegation that former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi's security was deliberately withdrawn to facilitate his assassination. Speaking in a candid conversation with her children Rahul and Priyanka about the creation of their family book 'Belonging: A Journey of Love,' she recounted raising concerns over his safety during his tours as opposition leader, when he travelled in an open jeep amid stone-pelting and protests at states ruled by opposition parties. She described those responsible for his protection as having failed to pay adequate attention to his security, recalling that Rahul had returned home after one such tour telling her, 'Mama, if we don't do something about Papa's security, I know I'm going to come back for his funeral very soon.' Sonia said the Bihar tour was the final trigger for her concerns. She then made a direct allegation: 'Papa's security was removed so that he got killed... It was done on purpose so that he got killed,' attributing this claim to herself in the shared video conversation.
items.title: Sonia Gandhi revisits Rajiv security withdrawal, alleges it was deliberate

items.summary: Fresh satellite imagery analysis by an Indian geospatial AI deep tech start-up incubated at FITT, IIT Delhi shows that construction of China's 60 GW Medog hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo (the Siang in India) is advanced and widespread. The report says the project lies near the McMahon Line, about 40 km to 50 km north of Arunachal Pradesh, and will include a tunnel across the river's famous 'Great U-Bend,' multiple power stations, and outlets before the river enters India.
items.title: Satellite Analysis Shows China's Medog Hydropower Project Advanced Near Arunachal Pradesh

items.summary:
The Conference of the Parties (COP) 31 concluded recently in Antalya, Türkiye. It was described as the longest COP and the first to be organized by two countries: Türkiye hosted while Australia served as President of Negotiations. Negotiations were extended by two days but drew accusations that backroom negotiations excluded all parties or lacked transparency about secret dealings. Some countries and NGOs branded it the worst COP.

The central sticking point mirrored the one at Brazil's COP30, where negotiators sought to explicitly mention phasing out fossil fuels in the cover text as a major outcome of COP31 talks. With the US absent, other major oil-producing countries blocked any statements on phasing out fossil fuels. Fossil fuels are now referred to as the "F" word while many countries continue investing heavily in their production. Major fossil fuel producers pushed electrification (the 35 by 35 goal of 35 per cent renewables by 2035) and carbon capture as effective steps toward eventual phaseout, according to the article.

The European Union broke consensus needed to approve the cover text at COPs, while roadmaps for phasing out fossil fuels are being released by several countries with their own strategies. The tyranny of consensus led again to failure at a COP, and climate finance issues continued struggling as well. Overall progress on climate mitigation was described as better but much slower than desirable, while adaptation struggled because it is neither ideal for global leadership nor attractive as an investment option for banks and financiers.

The article's author argues that headlines focused entirely on warming impacts, crossing thresholds, lack of political will, unwillingness to phase out fossil fuels, or insufficient climate finance. He noted no significant attention was paid to investing in innovations and training design engineers, doctors, and social scientists needed for solutions and adaptations across sectors such as agriculture, food, water, energy, transportation, buildings, and health.

On mitigation, the author said warming targets of 2 degrees Celsius from the Paris Agreement reduced to 1.5 degrees Celsius became rallying cries accelerating efforts and updating national commitments while countries struggled with socioeconomics, geopolitics, climate justice, and just transition issues. He characterized concepts like "super" El Niño as unscientific with no clear science explaining special impacts at local scales.

On adaptation, the author described programs as critical to blunt warming impacts but contextual, location- and sector-specific, focused on avoiding losses and inducing economic and ecological co-benefits rather than profits. He argued successful adaptations may reduce willingness to sustain financing while making them unclear investment options for banks and private financiers because resilience is foundational to ensuring risks do not disrupt development.

The author concluded that COPs should focus on climate solutions rather than aspirational statements, suggesting the tyranny of consensus may need to end so progress can be made with majority rule. He attributed these views to Raghu Murtugudde, Emeritus Professor at University of Maryland and Visiting Professor at Kotak School of Sustainability, IIT Kanpur.
items.title: COP31 Concludes in Antalya Without Fossil Fuel Phaseout Language

items.summary: Reuters reported on Tuesday that ousted Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina is planning to return to her country on December 16, after more than two years in exile in India. December 16 marks Bangladesh's Victory Day, commemorating the nation's liberation from Pakistan in 1971 following the Indo-Pakistan War. According to Reuters, Hasina has urged the government to arrange for her return via Biman Bangladesh Airlines, the state-owned carrier. Her spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali was quoted as saying that since she was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5, 2024, it is now the government's responsibility—having exiled her contrary to the Constitution—to make possible her return on Victory Day. Hasina fled to India in August 2024 after ruling for 16 years; her ouster followed weeks of widespread student-led protests against her government. In November 2025, she was sentenced to death by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal for crimes against humanity connected to a deadly crackdown on protesters in 2024. However, an unidentified Bangladesh minister told Reuters on Sunday that Hasina would be arrested and jailed upon return, adding that no official discussions had taken place with India about sending an aircraft to bring her back. On November 18, hundreds of paramilitary troops were deployed as talks of her return triggered clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks blamed on supporters of her banned Awami League party. Dhaka said it completed the legal procedures required to secure Hasina's return on November 14, with the final decision on extradition resting with New Delhi. The former prime minister reportedly requested a new passport and identity card from Dhaka, but the government has rejected the request, prompting protests by her supporters.
items.title: Ousted Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina Plans December 16 Return

items.summary:
Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has publicly set December 16 as the date for her return home, coinciding with the country's Victory Day. Her spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali told Reuters that she fled India after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule in August 2024 and is now calling on the government to arrange transport via Biman Bangladesh Airlines from Delhi back to Dhaka. Hasina has also requested a new passport and identity card, which Bangladeshi officials had previously rejected.

The planned return could heighten political and legal tensions since her Awami League party remains banned. A Bangladeshi minister told Reuters on Sunday that Hasina would be arrested upon entry and jailed, with no official discussions held with India about sending an aircraft to bring her back. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said the government wants India to honor its extradition treaty and return Hasina as a convict.

Hasina faces a death sentence in Bangladesh from a war crimes court that sentenced her in absentia in November 2024 for ordering a crackdown on protesters during the uprising. The United Nations reported up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest that forced her out of power. Hasina has denied the charges and said she is ready to fight the case once back in Bangladesh.
items.title: Sheikh Hasina Plans Return to Bangladesh on Victory Day, Requests Biman Flight from Delhi

items.summary: Parastoo Ahmadi, an Iranian singer, was reportedly flogged 74 times each along with four members of her production team after being convicted of offending public decency. According to reports from the Emtedad news website cited by local media on Monday (local time), the punishment was carried out in Qom, where a court had handed down the sentences in June, finding all five guilty of sharing online material it deemed obscene and immoral.
items.title: Iranian Singer Parastoo Ahmadi and Four Others Flogged for Performing Without Hijab

items.summary: Uttar Pradesh is expanding its technology infrastructure and incentives beyond Noida as HCLTech grows its Lucknow campus, seeking to create local employment, strengthen skills, and distribute technology investment across regions. For years the state's IT story has largely been a Noida story, with that city emerging as the main hub; the government now wants to take the ecosystem into cities such as Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, and Gorakhpur by expanding infrastructure, offering incentives, and building a talent pipeline. The expansion is taking shape through new Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) facilities, policy changes, and fresh investments by companies already operating in the state.
items.title: Uttar Pradesh Expands IT Infrastructure Beyond Noida

items.summary:
The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear on Wednesday renewed bail petitions filed by activists Sharjeel Imam and Umar Khalid challenging the Delhi High Court's refusal to grant them bail in a case under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. According to Press Trust of India, the pleas test prolonged UAPA detention as protected witnesses remain unexamined and a court-set deadline nears.

Imam and Khalid have been detained since 2020 after being booked on allegations that they were among the masterminds of the February 2020 northeast Delhi riots. The violence broke out during protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, and the National Register of Citizens, leaving 53 people dead and more than 700 injured according to PTI.

In his petition, Imam said the charge sheet was filed on September 25, 2020. It named 18 accused while the prosecution cited more than 900 witnesses, including 47 protected witnesses. He stated that despite spending six years and nine months as an undertrial prisoner, the prosecution had not examined a single witness.

Khalid also cited the failure to examine protected witnesses, arguing that once the one-year waiting period expires his continued imprisonment would violate Article 21 of the Constitution, which protects the right to life and personal liberty. Imam was arrested on August 25, 2020, and Khalid on September 13, 2020.

The Delhi High Court refused bail to both men on September 30, saying it was bound by "judicial discipline" and could not modify the Supreme Court's January 5 order. That order allowed the two accused to seek bail after the examination of protected witnesses or the expiry of one year, whichever came earlier.

The trial court had rejected their bail petitions for a third time on July 4, saying it had "no option but to follow" the Supreme Court's January 5 order and could neither consider the petitions nor grant relief. The high court noted that while denying bail in January, the Supreme Court described Khalid and Imam as the "ideological drivers" of the alleged conspiracy.

On September 2, a Delhi High Court division bench denied bail to both men; on January 5, the Supreme Court upheld that verdict but granted relief to co-accused Gulfisha Fatima, Meeran Haider, Shifa Ur Rehman, Mohammad Saleem Khan and Shadab Ahmad. A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and N V Anjaria had observed there was a case against Khalid and Imam under the UAPA at first sight.

On May 22, the Supreme Court granted six months' interim bail to co-accused Abdul Khalid Saifi and Tasleem Ahmad. It also referred to a larger bench the issue of prolonged imprisonment of undertrial prisoners under the UAPA because of the law's strict bail conditions. Other accused including activist Khalid Saifi and former Aam Aadmi Party councillor Tahir Hussain were also booked for their alleged involvement in the case, which is being investigated by the Delhi Police Special Cell.

According to the Supreme Court's cause list, a bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana is likely to hear the petitions. The Supreme Court will now consider Imam's and Khalid's renewed requests for bail based on the prosecution's failure to examine protected witnesses and the approaching expiry of the one-year period fixed by the court.
items.title: Supreme Court to Hear Sharjeel Imam, Umar Khalid Bail Pleas

items.summary:
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) are expected to announce their alliance for the upcoming Punjab assembly elections on Tuesday at a joint press conference scheduled for 1pm at BJP headquarters in New Delhi, according to news agency ANI. Union home minister Amit Shah, BJP chief Nitin Nambiar, and SAD supremo Sukhbir Singh Badal will attend the event.

The alliance revives ties between the two parties that ended their decades-old partnership in 2020 after the Akali Dal walked out of the National Democratic Alliance over the now-repealed farm laws. Under their previous arrangement, the BJP contested 23 of Punjab's 117 assembly seats while the SAD fought the remaining constituencies.

BJP sources indicated earlier that the party would contest a substantially higher number of seats than under the prior arrangement as it seeks to expand its political footprint in the state. The BJP has stepped up outreach with an aggressive campaign against drug addiction and opposition to religious conversions by missionaries among key planks, and has inducted leaders from other parties.

The alliance comes amid improved electoral performance for the BJP following its 2024 Lok Sabha elections, where it secured over 18% of votes in Punjab compared with the SAD's over 13%, per reports. The SAD, once a dominant regional force, has seen declining fortunes after the Aam Aadmi Party swept to power in the state during the 2022 assembly elections.
items.title: BJP and SAD to Reunite in Punjab Ahead of Assembly Elections

items.summary: At least four children were killed and 32 others injured after a speeding truck rammed into a stationary school bus on the Lucknow-Agra Expressway near Thathia area in Uttar Pradesh's Kannauj district around 6 am Tuesday, police said. The accident occurred when the Oriental Public School bus from Kaushambi was parked on the expressway shoulder to allow children to use the toilet; the truck struck it from behind and damaged its rear portion, according to Superintendent of Police Vinod Kumar. The bus was carrying 50 people, including students returning from an excursion to the Taj Mahal in Agra, with the injured group comprising eight school staff members and 24 students, police said. Responders—including police personnel, Uttar Pradesh Expressways Industrial Development Authority (UPEIDA) staff, and passing commuters—rushed to the scene and rescued children from the damaged bus before they were taken by ambulance to a medical college where doctors declared four of them dead. The deceased were identified as Aryan Chaurasia (14), son of Prem Kumar Chaurasia; Raziullah (16), son of Shamiullah; and Armaan (17) and Zaid Mirza (17), both sons of Riaz Ahmad, according to police. School manager Salman and one child in critical condition were referred to Kanpur for further treatment while the remaining injured students and staff members are undergoing treatment at the medical college, Kumar said. District Magistrate Ashutosh Mohan Agnihotri and SP Kumar visited the medical college to inquire about the injured's conditions, police reported.
items.title: Truck Ramming Stationary School Bus Kills 4 Children, Injures 32 in Kannauj

items.summary: According to Hindustan Times reporting from its newsdesk, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Shiromani Akali Dal are expected to announce their alliance in Punjab today. The report is attributed to HT's round-the-clock newsdesk team, which covers Indian politics and elections through reporters on the ground as well as official statements and other authoritative sources, with stories subject to editorial scrutiny before publication.
items.title: BJP, Akali Dal Likely to Announce Punjab Alliance Today

items.summary: Speaking with Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi ahead of the release of her memoir Belonging: A Journey Of Love, Sonia Gandhi recounted why she declined to become Prime Minister after the Congress-led alliance won the 2004 Lok Sabha election. She said she felt responsible for party workers who had campaigned across India and believed leaving after the campaign would let them down, though she also questioned whether her sense of duty shaped that reasoning and reflected on how holding power can make it easy to find reasons to keep it. Rahul Gandhi described the atmosphere in the room when his mother decided against taking the post, noting one person present was seen as the strongest choice while others had hoped for the position; he said some felt relief from her decision while others were happy she stepped aside. The discussion took place around the release of Belonging: A Journey Of Love, which Sonia wrote from her own memories with Rahul and Priyanka adding their recollections to give the stories new life. Rahul also discussed episodes left out of the book, including abuse and humiliation his mother endured after joining the Nehru-Gandhi family, attacks on her because she was born in Italy despite efforts to settle into Indian life, allegations that Rajiv Gandhi's security removal was deliberate so he would be killed with a warning before his Bihar trip, and a failed proposal surrounding his seventh birthday. Sonia said revisiting those years brought back laughter, happiness, and painful memories while describing her children as her greatest joy and strength.
items.title: Sonia Gandhi Recalls Turning Down 2004 PM Post in Memoir Discussion

items.summary: In a video interaction with his mother, Sonia Gandhi, and sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra while discussing her memoir 'Belonging,' Rahul Gandhi alleged that former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi's security was deliberately removed so he could be killed. The remarks revived Congress's long-standing accusation against the then-V.P. Singh government regarding the withdrawal of Rajiv Gandhi's protection. During their discussion, Sonia Gandhi recounted how Rahul joined his father on a 1991 trip to Bihar where stones were pelted at him and anti-him slogans shouted by crowds; when Rahul returned home he told her that if nothing was done about his father's security, she would soon return for his funeral. Rahul described the Bihar incident as the final straw and stated clearly that 'Papa's security was removed so that he got killed,' adding that it was not an accident but deliberately created to enable his death. He also mentioned having argued with his father over his own security. Meanwhile, Priyanka recalled how after Indira Gandhi's assassination, Sonia became paranoid about Rajiv's security and would check the barbed wire and wake sleeping guards. The Congress party has maintained that the withdrawal of Rajiv Gandhi's security was an operation of law.
items.title: Rahul Gandhi Alleges Rajiv Gandhi's Security Was Removed to Enable His Killing

items.summary: Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi alleged that the security of former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi was deliberately withdrawn in order to facilitate his killing. She made the remarks during a conversation with her children, Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi, about her book Belonging: A Journey of Love.
items.title: Sonia Gandhi Alleges Rajiv Gandhi's Security Was Deliberately Withdrawn to Facilitate His Killing

items.summary: Kerala Devaswom Minister K Muraleedharan said on Tuesday that a drop in Sabarimala pilgrims this year was caused by problems in the virtual queue booking system, with suspicions that slots were being booked in bulk and sold illegally. He stated that around 6,000 devotees per day are not showing up despite having secured bookings through the virtual queue. In response to these no-shows, Muraleedharan said instructions have been given to increase spot booking slots, though this requires approval from the Kerala High Court; he noted that permission has already been sought by the Travancore Devaswom Board (TDB). The minister added that the TDB is examining the matter and had sent a letter to State Home Minister asking them to investigate all aspects of suspected illegal slot sales, warning that anyone caught selling bookings illegally will face stringent action. He assured reporters that the identified booking system problem would be examined and resolved, while noting separately that devotees are turning up in greater numbers than usual during monthly poojas at the hill-top shrine.
items.title: Sabarimala Pilgrim Drop Attributed to Booking System Issues

items.summary: Saurav Das, co-convener of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), alleged that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from boarding a 1 am flight to London after his passport was flagged. According to news agency Press Trust of India (PTI), Das said he had been invited by the Oxford University Students' Union to participate in a panel discussion about the "cockroach movement" and claimed several other universities, including Cambridge, LSE, and Edinburgh, also extended invitations for him to speak on the topic. In posts on X, Das accused the Narendra Modi government of preventing his travel, stating he was invited by prestigious institutions but denied permission to attend events discussing the cockroach movement. He questioned why the government would object to an educated young person participating in intellectual discussions at international universities and criticized the administration's functioning, including its inability to expand the cabinet due to ministers refusing to resign. Das also attacked fugitive businessmen Nirav Modi and Vijay Mallya while criticizing the alleged action. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke similarly condemned the incident on X, suggesting that someone in power was jealous of Das receiving an invitation from Oxford. Despite being unable to board his scheduled flight, Das said he would not be discouraged from continuing his work and intended to travel to London, Paris, and other international destinations in the future. The report does not include a response from the government or immigration authorities regarding the alleged passport flagging.
items.title: Cockroach Janta Party's Saurav Das Alleges Delhi Airport Passport Flagging Blocked London Trip

items.summary: At a high-level United Nations Security Council briefing on Monday, India's Permanent Representative Harish Parvathaneni called for an immediate halt to attacks on commercial shipping and seafarers in the Black Sea, saying safe navigation through international waterways must be restored at the earliest. Speaking of the Russia-Ukraine conflict now in its fifth year, he said it was having far-reaching consequences due to interconnected global supply chains, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi noting that "the world has to move from 'endless war to the end of war.'" Parvathaneni emphasized that conflicts exacerbate food insecurity by disrupting agriculture and hindering humanitarian access, with consequences extending through energy, fertiliser, transport and agricultural trade while disproportionately impacting the Global South. He highlighted the Black Sea region's importance to global food security, noting that the region combined with India accounted for almost a fifth of global cereal production (3 million people; 04), and that Russia and Ukraine together accounted for nearly a quarter of global exports of wheat, maize and barley. The envoy cited India's humanitarian assistance—wheat supplies to Afghanistan, rice to Sudan, and aid to Palestine—and referenced External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar's observation at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting that fertiliser shortages stem partly from the Black Sea and partly from the Gulf and Red Sea. Recalling the 1943 Bengal famine that killed over three million people in India, Parvathaneni stressed the human cost of distant conflicts. He detailed attacks on merchant vessels: the MV Omorfi attacked on 18 July with an Indian crew member lost; the MV Royad Mammadov under attack in October with three Indian nationals aboard; and two additional ships (MV Golden Leo and MV AGN RAGNAR) struck, resulting in four dead and two missing Indian seafarers. He thanked partner countries for repatriating injured seafarers while reiterating the call to end targeting of commercial shipping and restore safe navigation.
items.title: India Urges UN Security Council to End Black Sea Shipping Attacks and Restore Safe Navigation
